Gabriel (Angel)
GAY-bree-ul
proper noun (angelology)
Hebrew Gavri'el (man of God or God is my strength). The angelic messenger named in Daniel (8:16; 9:21) and Luke (1:19, 26). The herald-angel who interprets visions and announces the births of John the Baptist and the Lord Jesus.

📖 Biblical Definition

Hebrew Gavri'el (man of God or God is my strength), the angelic messenger named in four canonical passages. (1) Daniel 8:16, where Gabriel is commanded to make Daniel understand the vision of the ram and the goat. (2) Daniel 9:21-23, where Gabriel comes to Daniel at the time of the evening sacrifice to give him understanding of the prophecy of the seventy weeks. (3) Luke 1:19, where Gabriel announces to Zacharias the coming birth of John the Baptist, identifying himself: I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings. (4) Luke 1:26-38, where Gabriel is sent to the virgin Mary in Nazareth to announce the conception and birth of the Lord Jesus (the Annunciation), declaring Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee... thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS. Gabriel is the herald-angel, the interpreter of visions and the announcer of the two most consequential births in redemptive history (the forerunner and the Messiah). He stands in the presence of God (Luke 1:19), among the highest of the angelic host. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine of Gabriel: a real created angel, the messenger and herald of God, the interpreter of prophetic visions and the announcer of the births of John and Jesus — a creature in the service of God's redemptive purposes, not an object of worship or devotion.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Hebrew man of God / God is my strength; the angelic messenger named in Daniel (8:16; 9:21) and Luke (1:19, 26); the herald-angel who interprets visions and announces the births of John the Baptist and the Lord Jesus (the Annunciation).

GABRIEL, proper n. (angelology; Hebrew Gavri'el, man of God / God is my strength) The angelic messenger named in four canonical passages. Daniel 8:16 (commanded to make Daniel understand the vision); Daniel 9:21-23 (giving understanding of the seventy weeks); Luke 1:19 (announcing John the Baptist's birth to Zacharias, I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God); Luke 1:26-38 (the Annunciation to the virgin Mary, announcing the conception and birth of the Lord Jesus). The herald-angel, interpreter of prophetic visions, announcer of the births of the forerunner and the Messiah. Stands in the presence of God among the highest of the angelic host.

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 1:19 — "And the angel answering said unto him, I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings."

Luke 1:26-27 — "And in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."

Daniel 9:21-22 — "Yea, whiles I was speaking in prayer, even the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening oblation. And he informed me, and talked with me."

Daniel 8:16 — "And I heard a man's voice between the banks of Ulai, which called, and said, Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Gabriel is a created angel in the service of God's redemptive purposes; the principal corruptions are angel-veneration (Catholic and new-age) and the rationalist dismissal of the biblical angelic messengers.

expand to see more

Gabriel as a proper name does not undergo lexical corruption. As with Michael, the two principal mishandlings are opposite. The Catholic and new-age tendency exalts Gabriel into an object of veneration and devotion; this contradicts the biblical refusal of angel-worship (Revelation 22:8-9). The rationalist tendency dismisses the biblical angelic messengers as mythological. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: Gabriel is a real created angel, the herald-messenger of God who interprets prophetic visions and announces the births of John the Baptist and the Lord Jesus. The Annunciation (Luke 1:26-38) is one of the great moments of redemptive history, and Gabriel's role as the announcing herald is a substantive part of the incarnation narrative — but Gabriel is a creature in God's service, not an object of worship; the glory belongs to the God who sent him and to the Christ whose birth he announced.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Gavri'el (man of God / God is my strength); Daniel 8:16; 9:21; Luke 1:19, 26; the herald-angel and interpreter of visions; announcer of the births of John and Jesus.
